questions.question: Urbanization is the process by which
choices: cities lose all connections to rural regions
a growing share of a population lives in urban areas
farms replace transportation networks
a country's population becomes evenly distributed

questions.question: What is a central business district (CBD)?
choices: A rural area with few services
A boundary used only for national elections
A city's major concentration of commercial and office activity
A zone reserved for agriculture

questions.question: A city expands outward as residents move to homes farther from the center. This pattern is often called
choices: counterurbanization
urban renewal
industrialization
suburbanization

questions.question: Why can access to public transit influence where people live and work?
choices: Transit changes travel time and the set of places people can reach
Transit determines a city's climate
Transit removes the need for land-use planning
Transit makes all neighborhoods identical

questions.question: A neighborhood gains new investment and housing costs rise, pushing some long-time residents to move. This process may be described as
choices: rural depopulation
gentrification
desertification
deindustrialization

questions.question: Which condition most directly contributes to an urban heat island?
choices: A city's elevation always increases its temperature
Urban areas receive no rainfall
Buildings and paved surfaces absorb and retain more heat than nearby vegetated areas
Trees release heat into every street

questions.question: A planner wants to reduce flood risk in a rapidly growing city. Which measure is most likely to help?
choices: Cover open land with more pavement
Build homes only in low-lying flood zones
Remove drainage channels without alternatives
Protect wetlands and use permeable surfaces to absorb stormwater

questions.question: Why might informal settlements develop at the edges of a fast-growing city?
choices: Housing and infrastructure may not expand as quickly or affordably as the population
Residents prefer to live without access to services
Cities have no land-use decisions
Urban migration always results from one cause

questions.question: Which data would best help compare access to parks across neighborhoods?
choices: The number of city council meetings held each year
The distance or travel time from residents' homes to public green space
The height of the tallest downtown building
The city's average annual rainfall alone

questions.question: A city places homes, shops, and services near a train station. What goal does this pattern often support?
choices: Greater dependence on long car trips
Lower access to public transportation
More compact, transit-oriented development
Separation of all daily activities

questions.question: Why can zoning decisions affect social and economic patterns within a city?
choices: They determine the national currency
They make land values unrelated to location
They eliminate the need for transportation
They shape which activities and buildings are allowed in different areas

questions.question: A new highway shortens commute times for one suburb but divides a nearby neighborhood. What should a planning review include?
choices: Both transportation benefits and the distribution of social and environmental costs
Only the projected vehicle speed
Only the highway's construction materials
A decision to exclude affected residents from the analysis

questions.question: Which factor is most likely to attract businesses to a particular urban location?
choices: Distance from every worker and customer
Access to customers, workers, transportation, and supporting services
Lack of reliable utilities
A location with no connection to suppliers

questions.question: An urban population grows quickly, but the number of schools and water connections stays the same. What challenge may result?
choices: Population density automatically declines
The city's tax base must disappear
Public services may not meet residents' needs
The region becomes rural

questions.question: Which strategy can improve a neighborhood's walkability?
choices: Separate homes from all daily services
Remove shade and pedestrian crossings
Require a car for every local trip
Create connected sidewalks, safe crossings, and nearby destinations

questions.question: A city measures the number of residents per square kilometer. What is it measuring?
choices: Population density
Population growth rate
Natural increase
Net migration

questions.question: A downtown office district loses employers, while warehouses and service businesses grow in a nearby area. What geographic idea helps explain this shift?
choices: A permanent uniform pattern of city development
Changes in land use and economic activity over time
A change in latitude
A movement of tectonic plates

questions.question: Why should urban development plans consider residents' access to clean water and sanitation?
choices: They matter only in rural regions
They are unrelated to city infrastructure
These services affect health, opportunity, and quality of life
They make population data unnecessary

questions.question: A city is comparing two housing plans. Plan A adds more units near existing transit; Plan B expands into farmland far from services. Which comparison is most complete?
choices: Compare only the number of buildings
Assume the larger land area always costs less
Ignore access to jobs and public services
Compare affordability, travel, infrastructure costs, land use, and environmental effects

questions.question: Why do some cities adopt mixed-use zoning?
choices: It can place housing, shops, and services closer together
It prevents people from walking between destinations
It requires every neighborhood to have the same density
It eliminates the need to manage traffic
